audioScript: Would you be willing to switch presentation slots with me? I have a conflict Tuesday.

choices.text: I'd like to help, but Tuesday's worse for me.
I've never seen a presentation quite like that one.
The conflict was resolved peacefully.
Tuesday is my favorite day of the week.

explanation: The key politely refuses because swapping would put the listener on Tuesday, while "The conflict was resolved peacefully" treats "conflict" as a dispute.

audioScript: Looks like the professor really went out of her way to give detailed comments.

choices.text: The details are all in the appendix.
My comments in class were brief.
She went out the side door after class.
She must have spent hours on every paper.

explanation: The key agrees by inferring the effort involved, while "She went out the side door" takes "went out of her way" literally.

audioScript: I heard the midterm has been moved up to this Thursday.

choices.text: There goes my plan to study this weekend.
I heard it on the radio, too.
I moved into a new apartment last month.
Thursday's forecast calls for rain.

explanation: The key recognizes that the earlier date ruins a weekend study plan, while "I moved into a new apartment" echoes "moved."

audioScript: The professor's comments say my argument is solid but my evidence is thin.

choices.text: The library has thinner textbooks than it used to.
Her comments were posted on Monday.
My argument with my roommate is over.
So you need stronger sources, not a new thesis.

explanation: The key interprets the feedback correctly, while "My argument with my roommate" uses "argument" to mean a quarrel.

audioScript: If I were you, I'd hold off on declaring a major until you've taken more classes.

choices.text: I'll hold the door for you.
Classes were canceled due to snow.
But wouldn't waiting delay my graduation?
Majors are listed in the catalog.

explanation: The key raises a relevant concern about the advice, while "I'll hold the door for you" misreads "hold off."

audioScript: I didn't expect so many people to show up for the optional review.

choices.text: Everyone's nervous about the new exam format.
The optional readings are listed online.
Many people expected rain today.
I'll show you the review later tonight.

explanation: The key explains the surprising turnout, while "I'll show you the review later" echoes "show" and "review."

audioScript: I was hoping you could explain what you meant by 'underdeveloped' in your comments.

choices.text: The development office is downstairs.
My comments are usually quite short.
I meant to email you about it yesterday.
Your second section makes claims without support.

explanation: The key clarifies the comment as requested, while "The development office is downstairs" plays on "underdeveloped."

audioScript: Do you want to join our study group, or would you rather go it alone?

choices.text: I focus better on my own, but thanks.
I'd rather have tea, thanks.
The group project was a big success.
I went alone to the concert last night.

explanation: The key politely declines with a reason, while "I'd rather have tea" reuses "rather" for an unrelated choice.

audioScript: The professor seems a lot more relaxed since she submitted her book manuscript.

choices.text: She submitted our grades late.
Her first book is in the campus library now.
Relaxing music helps me study at night.
It must have been weighing on her all semester.

explanation: The key infers why she seems relaxed, while "Her first book is in the campus library" ignores that it was only just submitted.

audioScript: Office hours are pretty useless if you don't come with specific questions.

choices.text: Specifically, the hours are two to four on Tuesdays.
True—I once sat there with nothing to ask.
The review questions are on page twelve.
Her office has a useful bookshelf.

explanation: The key agrees with a personal example, while "Specifically, the hours are two to four" echoes "specific" and "hours."

audioScript: The registrar said my transfer credits didn't count toward my major.

choices.text: Can you appeal, or is that decision final?
I counted the credits twice to be sure.
Majors are declared in sophomore year.
Transfer to the blue line at the next station.

explanation: The key asks a relevant follow-up about options, while "Transfer to the blue line" uses "transfer" in a travel sense.

audioScript: I'm having trouble following the lectures—any chance you'd share your notes?

choices.text: There's a chance of rain later this afternoon.
I'm following that author online these days.
I took notes in high school, too.
They're messy, but you're welcome to photograph them.

explanation: The key agrees to share with a caveat, while "There's a chance of rain later" reuses "chance" literally.

audioScript: It's frustrating that two of my required courses meet at exactly the same time.

choices.text: Time really flies when you're busy.
We met at the same café.
Is either one offered in the summer session?
Required reading is listed on the course page.

explanation: The key suggests a way around the conflict, while "We met at the same café" echoes "met" and "same."

audioScript: We should probably touch base with the TA before we change the project scope.

choices.text: Agreed—she might not approve such a big shift.
The project changed hands last year.
I touched the base of the lamp by accident.
Microscopes are used in biology labs.

explanation: The key agrees with the idiom's meaning of checking in, while "I touched the base of the lamp" takes "touch base" literally.

audioScript: Wow, you finished your thesis draft a whole month ahead of schedule.

choices.text: The schedule changes every month.
I wanted time for my advisor's revisions.
My thesis is on bird migration patterns.
I'll finish it sometime next month, hopefully.

explanation: The key explains why the draft was finished early, while "I'll finish it sometime next month" contradicts the fact that it is already done.
